sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Śani** ​(*sani*) — ‌Justice, Saturn, ‌Karma · ​"The Slow ​One" — ​Saturn as ​the lord ​of karma, ‌justice, discipline, ​and time ​— ‌belongs to ​the Sanskrit ‌tradition, where ​it is ‌catalogued under ​the domain ​"Justice, Saturn, ​Karma". The ​name means ​""The Slow ‌One" ​— Saturn ‌as the ​lord of ‌karma, justice, ​discipline, and ‌time"[^1].

Śani ​is the ‌most feared ​of the ​nine planets: ‌Saturn ‌as the ‌auditor of ​karma, whose ​slow passage ‌through the ​zodiac delivers ​every deed's ‌return — ​never early, ​never late, ‌and ​never, ever ‌argued with. ​India loves ​him exactly ​as much ​as it ‌fears him, ‌which is ​to say, ‌enormously.[^2]

PuniCodex ​restores ​the name ‌as **Śani** ‌and serves ‌its temple ‌at [śani.com](https://xn--ani-bza.com). ​The original ‌carries both ​stress and ​vowel length, ​and exactly ‌one ​historically valid ​Unicode restoration ​exists, which ‌places the ​name in ​Tier 1. ​The plain ‌ASCII form ​*sani* survives ‌as a ​modern ‌convenience imposed ​by the ‌early domain-name ‌system; the ​restoration, not ​the fallback, ​is the ​form the ‌project defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The ​name is ‌attested ‌in Devanagari ​as ​**शनि**. Etymologically ​it ​means ""The ​Slow ‌One" — ​Saturn ​as the ‌lord ​of karma, ‌justice, ​discipline, and ‌time"[^1].

​The ASCII ​form ​*sani* survives ​only ​because the ‌early domain-name ​system ‌could not ​carry ‌diacritics; it ​is ‌a technological ​compromise, ‌not an ​ancient ​spelling. The ‌Unicode ‌restoration **Śani** ‌recovers ​the full ​diacritic ‌detail of ​the ​scholarly transliteration ‌directly ​in the ​address ‌bar. The ​original ‌carries both ​stress ​and vowel ​length, ​and exactly ‌one ‌historically valid ​Unicode ‌restoration exists, ​which ​places the ‌name ‌in Tier ‌1.

‌The letter-by-letter ​transformation ‌runs:

- ​**s** ​→ **Ś** ​— ‌Palatal ś ​(IAST)
- ​**a** ​→ **a** ‌— ​Same
- ​**n** ​→ **n** ‌— ​Same
- ‌**i** ​→ **i** ‌— ​Same

The ‌project ‌holds the ​domain ​**śani.com** (xn--ani-bza.com) ​as ​the canonical ‌home ‌of this ​name[^2].

sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The ​reconstructed pronunciation ‌of ‌the ​name is ​**/ɕɐ.ni/** ​— ​Reconstructed Sanskrit.[^1]

​For ‌the ​modern speaker, ​the ‌closest approximation ​is: ‌SHUH-nee ​— soft ‌palatal ​sh, ​short and ​even.

​Kindred ​and historical ‌forms ​of the ‌name:

​- ‌**Devanagari** — ​शनि
‌- ​**IAST standard** ‌— ​Śani
​- **Hindi ‌speech** ‌— Shani
‌- ​**Owned ​form** — ‌Śani

​Sanskrit ​śani — ‌"the ​slow ​one" — ‌begins ​with the ‌palatal ​ś ​(IAST's acute-accented ​s) ​and ‌the short ‌a ​and ‌i. The ​restoration ​keeps the ‌ś ‌that ‌English writes ‌"sh": ​Śani, ‌the slow ​planet, ​whose ​very name ‌is ​a warning ​about ​haste. ‌The ś ​is ​the ​palatal sibilant, ‌made ​at ‌the roof ​of ‌the mouth ​farther ‌forward ‌than sh ​— ​the ​sound English ​approximates ‌but ‌never quite ​keeps.

sections.body:
Śani ​is ‌the most ‌feared ​of ​the nine ​planets: ​Saturn ​as ‌the auditor ​of ​karma, ‌whose slow ​passage ‌through ​the ‌zodiac delivers ​every ​deed's ​return — ​never ​early, ‌never ​late, and ‌never, ​ever ‌argued with. ​India ‌loves ​him ‌exactly as ​much ​as ‌it fears ‌him, ‌which ​is ​to say, ‌enormously.[^1]

​### ​Sade Sati

‌The ​seven-and-a-half ​years ‌of his ​transit ‌over ​your ​moon — ​India's ​most-dreaded ‌astrological season.

‌### ​The ‌Auditor

​Karma's bookkeeper: ​no ‌bribe, ‌no appeal, ‌no ‌clerical ​error ‌— only ​the ​account.

​### Son ‌of ​the ​Sun

​Sūrya's estranged ‌son ​— ​the shadow ​the ‌light ​itself ‌begot.

### ​The ‌Crow

​His vāhana: ‌the ‌dark ​bird ​that sees ​what ​others ‌will not ‌look ​at.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Śani's myths ​are about the ‌impossibility of ‌escaping consequence — ​even for gods, ​and especially ​for kings.[^1]

### ​The Shadow of ​the Sun ‌(The Birth)

Born ​of Sūrya and ​Chhāyā — ‌"Shadow," the substitute-wife ​the sun's true ‌wife left ​in her place ‌— Śani was ​the son ​the light refused ​to look at. ​His gaze ​fell so baleful ‌that his own ​father's skin darkened ‌at the ​meeting. The Purāṇas ‌make the estrangement ​permanent: the ‌planet of justice ​is the sun's ‌shadow-child, and ​no amount of ​brilliance exempts the ‌family from ‌audit.[^2]

### Even ‌the Gods Are ​Judged (The ​Gaze)

His stories ‌form a single ​syllabus: when ​Śani's gaze fell ‌on Śiva, the ​great god ​was made to ‌wander as a ​beggar; on Hanumān, ‌the mighty ​one was pressed ​until he learned ​humility; on ​Rāma's line, even ‌the righteous king's ‌fortune bowed. ​The Hanumān legend ‌adds the one ​counter: devotion ​freely given is ‌the only shield ‌Śani honors ‌— the one ‌god who bows ​to bhakti.

‌### Sade Sati ​(The Season)

The ​living myth ​is the calendar: ‌when Saturn transits ​the sign before, ​of, and ​after your natal ‌moon — seven ​and a ​half years — ​the astrologers warn ‌of Sade ​Sati, the season ‌of testing. Careers ​stall, elders ‌ail, patience thins ​— and the ‌remedy prescribed ‌is the same ​everywhere: sesame oil, ​iron, crows ​fed, and Śani's ​Saturday fast. The ‌most-followed planetary ‌observance in India ​is his.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
Śani is ​the god of "later." ‌Every tradition has a ‌debt-collector, but his genius ​is slowness: the audit ​arrives when the deeds ​are half-forgotten, itemized ​to the day. He ​asks the only question ‌that matters at midlife: ​not what did you ​build, but what did ‌you balance — and ​are you ready ‌for the season when ​the slow planet comes ‌to check?

The open ​shrine at Shingnapur is ​the whole doctrine in ​stone: no roof, ​no walls, a black ​boulder under the same ‌sky he rules. You ​do not contain Saturn; ‌you stand under him ​honestly, doors unlocked, ‌accounts straight. The doorless ​village trusts the audit. ‌That is the only ​prayer he reads.

The ‌remedies are worth reading ​closely: sesame oil, ​iron, the feeding of ‌crows, the Saturday fast ‌— not magic but ‌discipline, small weekly acts ​of humility calibrated to ​his tempo. Śani is ‌appeased by exactly ​what he represents: patience, ​repeated, in small measures, ‌for seven and a ​half years if necessary. ​The cure and the ‌god are the ​same medicine.

The astrologers' ‌caution is not terror ​but timing: Sade Sati ​ends, as surely as ​it begins, and the ​households that keep ‌the small disciplines through ‌it emerge, the tradition ​says, tempered like iron ‌that stayed in the ​fire long enough. Śani ​does not punish; he ‌anneals. The slow ‌planet's real gift is ‌what patience makes of ‌the patient.

The doorless ​village understood this centuries ‌ago. You do not ​lock out the ​auditor; you live so ​that the audit is ‌boring.

His temple etiquette ​is the final lesson: ​oil poured, iron touched, ​crows fed before ‌breakfast, and then the ​week begins — small ​debts paid in advance ​against the slow account. ‌India has refined the ​art of living ‌under Saturn into a ​weekly hygiene, and it ‌works exactly as intended: ​the audit, when it ‌comes, finds everything already ‌in order.

Slow is ​not the opposite ​of just; it is ​how justice travels when ​it intends to be ‌exact. The planet keeps ‌his time; the accounts ​keep theirs.[^1]
